title: The Mapmaker Who Invented Brazilian Identity
event_summary: A group of tailors, soldiers, and artisans — many of them mixed-race or formerly enslaved — launched the Conjuração Baiana (Bahian Conspiracy), posting handwritten pamphlets across Salvador demanding an independent republic, free trade, racial equality, and the abolition of slavery. The movement's intellectual architect was Cipriano Barata, a surgeon and mapmaker who had absorbed French Revolutionary ideas and translated them into a radical vision of multiracial democracy unprecedented in the Americas. Portuguese authorities arrested dozens, and four of the poorest conspirators — the tailors João de Deus, Lucas Dantas, Manuel Faustino, and Luís Gonzaga — were publicly hanged and dismembered in November 1799.
why_forgotten: Brazilian national mythology long preferred the elite-led Inconfidência Mineira of 1789 and its martyred hero Tiradentes as the founding independence narrative, because its leaders were white professionals. The Bahian revolt, driven by Black and mixed-race working-class men demanding racial equality alongside independence, was deliberately minimized by a slaveholding society uncomfortable with its implications. Portuguese colonial censorship destroyed many primary documents, and even after independence, Brazilian historians avoided centering enslaved and Afro-Brazilian agency.
why_it_matters: The Conjuração Baiana was the first movement in the Americas to explicitly demand both national independence and full racial equality simultaneously, anticipating arguments that would take another century to gain traction. Its suppression revealed the template colonial powers would repeatedly use: co-opting independence movements while stripping them of their radical egalitarian content. Brazil's ongoing struggle with systemic racism and the persistent erasure of Afro-Brazilian contributions to the nation's founding trace directly back to the deliberate silencing of this moment.
